posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: High-scoring compliance pain post with three ICP prospects engaging — validate the 'explainability' problem as the real blocker, not AI itself, and plant the idea that the gap is solvable without retreating from AI entirely
posts.draft_comment: The ban isn't the interesting part — it's what it reveals. Regulators don't need AI to disappear, they need an audit trail they can follow without a data scientist in the room. Most analytics tools were never built to explain themselves, and AI just made that gap impossible to ignore. Wonder how many other teams are quietly doing the same thing right now.

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO frustrated with Power BI adoption failure — validate the trust problem as the real blocker, not the tool, with ICP buyers already engaged in the thread
posts.draft_comment: The trust problem is almost always harder than the build problem. Eighteen months of engineering and your finance team still defaults to the spreadsheet they've trusted for years — that's not a training issue, that's a credibility gap the dashboard never closed. The numbers have to earn their place, and most tools don't help with that at all. What would it have taken for them to actually quote a figure from it in the room?

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Innovation Director at NorthStar Retail) engaging on a self-service BI pain post — validate the 'who owns truth' framing, add the layer that the problem isn't access to data, it's absence of shared definitions
posts.draft_comment: Three definitions of revenue is actually the norm, not the exception — most teams don't discover the disagreement until someone quotes a number in a board meeting and gets challenged. The licence was never the blocker. It's that self-service BI hands people a brush but nobody's agreed on what the painting should look like. Who in your org is actually empowered to settle those definition disputes when they surface?

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO framing AI hallucinations as a security risk with a CEO prospect engaging — validate the reframe, add the trust-chain insight that makes it concrete
posts.draft_comment: The framing here is exactly right and I think it changes the conversation. Most teams treat a hallucinated number as a data quality problem — something to clean up. But the real exposure is downstream: the decision gets made, the audit trail points to 'the AI said so,' and nobody owns it. Who's actually accountable when the model was confident and wrong?

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: ICP prospect (COO at Sterling Consulting) engaging with CEO frustration about unusable BI — validate the structural problem, add the insight that 'self-service' is a design failure not a training problem
posts.draft_comment: The £200k isn't even the painful part — it's the six months of 'we just need more training' before anyone admits it was never built for them. Most BI tools assume the person asking the question and the person who can answer it are the same person. They're almost never the same person in a 50-person business. What would it even look like if the tool was designed around the question, not the query?

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director at a mid-market industrial firm exposing a data governance/trust problem — validate the culture insight and add the layer about what actually breaks first
posts.draft_comment: Three teams, three filter choices, one meeting where the CFO loses faith in the whole system. That's not a data problem, that's a trust problem — and once it's broken it takes way longer to fix than whatever caused it. The AI point is right too. No amount of smarter tooling patches a situation where nobody agreed on what 'revenue' means in the first place. How long did it take before anyone noticed the numbers had drifted?

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Director of Operations at Summit Group) engaging on dashboard bloat — validate the 47-to-5 insight, add the 'why dashboards get bloated in the first place' layer, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: 47 KPIs is usually a political problem dressed up as a measurement problem — everyone wanted their metric on the board, so nobody said no. The 10% to 85% usage jump after cutting to 5 is the real signal here. Most teams think more coverage means more value, but I think it's the opposite: the moment a dashboard tries to serve everyone, it genuinely serves no one. What was the hardest metric to cut?

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director surfacing a real adoption failure with shadow AI as the punchline — validate the 'nobody knows what to ask' problem as a design flaw, not a training problem
posts.draft_comment: The 12% number is brutal but honest. 'Nobody knows what to ask' isn't a change management problem — it's the product telling you it was built for people who already know what they need. Shadow AI filling the gap makes total sense when the sanctioned tool puts the burden of knowing on the user. What would it take for Copilot to meet people where their actual question starts?
